screens.body: Imagine printing the numbers 1 to 100 without a loop — that's 100 lines of nearly identical code. A loop repeats a block of code for you: write it once, run it as many times as you need. Loops are how programs do repetitive work without repetitive writing.
screens.heading: Why loops exist

screens.body: A while loop repeats as long as its condition stays true. Check the condition, run the body, repeat. The critical rule: something inside the body must move toward ending the loop — usually incrementing a counter. If nothing changes, the loop runs forever. That's called an infinite loop, and every programmer has made one.
screens.heading: while: repeat until done
screens.keyPoint: while repeats while true — always change the counter.

screens.body: The for loop is built for counting. It packs three things into one line: where to start (int i = 0), when to stop (i < 3), and how to step (i++). The body runs once per value of i. When you know how many times to repeat, for is the natural choice.

check.question: How many times does "Hi" print below?

screens.heading: for: the counting loop
screens.keyPoint: for packs start, stop, and step into one line.

screens.body: Use for when you know the count up front — 'do this 10 times.' Use while when you're waiting for something to change — 'keep reading until the file ends,' 'ask until the answer is valid.' If you catch yourself writing a while with a counter, a for is probably cleaner.

check.question: Keep asking until the user types a valid answer — use…

screens.heading: for vs while
screens.keyPoint: for counts; while waits for a change.

screens.body: A loop can live inside another loop — that's nesting. The inner loop runs to completion for EVERY single round of the outer loop. If the outer runs 2 times and the inner runs 3 times, the inner body runs 2 × 3 = 6 times. Nested loops draw grids, tables, and patterns.

check.question: Outer runs 2×, inner runs 3× — the inner body runs…

screens.heading: Nested loops: a loop inside a loop
screens.keyPoint: Inner completes fully for each outer round.

screens.body: Two keywords steer loops from inside. break exits the loop immediately — done, stop repeating. continue skips the rest of this round and jumps to the next one. Use them sparingly: a loop with too many breaks and continues gets hard to follow.
screens.heading: break and continue
screens.keyPoint: break exits; continue skips to the next round.

screens.body: The most common loop bug is the off-by-one error: running one time too many or too few. for (i = 0; i < 5; i++) runs 5 times (0–4), but i <= 5 runs 6 times. Java counts from 0, so 'less than the length' (<) is usually right and 'less than or equal' (<=) usually overshoots by one.
screens.heading: Off-by-one: the classic bug
screens.keyPoint: < vs <= is the difference between right and off-by-one.
